title: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
description: Compare the three major versions of HTTP, understanding how each solved the limitations of its predecessor and what that means for real-world performance.

data.text: HTTP is the protocol that powers the web. Every time you load a webpage, click a link, or submit a form, your browser speaks HTTP to a server. Over the past two decades, HTTP has gone through three major revisions, each one designed to fix the performance and scalability problems of the previous version.

Understanding HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 is not just academic trivia. These versions directly affect page load times, battery life on mobile devices, and how servers handle thousands of simultaneous users. Knowing when and why each version exists helps you make better decisions about infrastructure, CDN configuration, and API design.
The Problem HTTP/1.1 Was Built to Solve

HTTP/1.0, introduced in 1996, opened a new TCP connection for every single request. If a webpage needed an HTML file, three CSS files, and five images, that meant nine separate connections. Each connection required its own TCP handshake and TLS negotiation, adding significant latency.

HTTP/1.1, released in 1999, introduced persistent connections. The same TCP socket could now handle multiple requests sequentially, reducing handshake overhead. This was a meaningful improvement, but it created a new bottleneck: only one request could be in flight at a time per connection.
Head-of-Line Blocking in HTTP/1.1

Because HTTP/1.1 processes requests sequentially, a slow response blocks everything behind it. If Request 1 is a large image that takes 500 milliseconds to download, Requests 2 through 10 must wait, even if the server already has them ready. This is called head-of-line blocking.

items: Only one request at a time per TCP connection
A slow resource delays all subsequent requests on that connection
Browsers opened 6 to 8 parallel connections per domain to work around this
Multiple parallel connections increased TCP congestion and TLS overhead
Headers are sent as plain text and repeated on every request, wasting bandwidth

data.title: Real-World Example
data.text: Imagine a restaurant with one waiter. The waiter takes your order, delivers it, then takes the next table's order. If your food takes 20 minutes, every table behind you waits, even if their food is ready. This is exactly what happens with HTTP/1.1 connections.
HTTP/2: Binary Framing and Multiplexing

HTTP/2, standardized in 2015 as RFC 7540, kept the same semantics as HTTP/1.1. URLs, methods, status codes, and headers all work exactly the same way. The difference is entirely in how data is framed and transported.

HTTP/2 replaces plain-text messages with a binary framing layer. Every request and response is split into small frames that are interleaved on a single TCP connection. This means the browser can send ten requests at once, and the server can send their responses in any order without any single response blocking another.
Key Features of HTTP/2

items: Multiplexing: multiple requests and responses share one TCP connection simultaneously
Binary framing: messages are encoded as binary frames for more efficient parsing
Header compression: HPACK compresses repeated headers, reducing overhead significantly
Server push: servers can proactively send resources before the browser requests them
Stream prioritization: browsers can tell the server which resources are most important
Requires HTTPS in all major browsers

data.text: Header Compression with HPACK

In HTTP/1.1, every request repeats headers like cookies, user agents, and accept headers. On a page with 50 requests, those kilobytes of repeated headers add up. HPACK solves this with two techniques: a static dictionary of common headers and dynamic table compression that remembers headers seen on previous requests.

data.title: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 Header Overhead
data.code:
# HTTP/1.1: Headers repeated on every request (plain text)
GET /style.css HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Cookie: session=abc123
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Accept: text/css
...

GET /app.js HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Cookie: session=abc123
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Accept: application/javascript
...

# HTTP/2: Headers compressed via HPACK
Headers for /style.css: ~40 bytes
Headers for /app.js:     ~35 bytes

data.text: HTTP/3: QUIC and the End of TCP Head-of-Line Blocking

HTTP/3, standardized in 2022 as RFC 9114, is the most significant change in the protocol's history. Instead of running over TCP, HTTP/3 uses QUIC, a transport protocol built on UDP. This change eliminates head-of-line blocking at the transport layer entirely.

The motivation is straightforward. In HTTP/2, a single lost TCP packet blocks the entire connection, even if other streams have data ready. QUIC solves this by treating each request as an independent stream. If a packet carrying Stream 1 is lost, Stream 2 can continue delivering data without waiting.

items: Runs over QUIC instead of TCP, removing transport-level head-of-line blocking
Built-in TLS 1.3 encryption; no separate TLS handshake required
Faster connection establishment with 0-RTT and 1-RTT handshakes
Connection migration preserves active sessions when switching networks
UDP-based implementation lives in user space, allowing faster protocol updates

data.title: Why UDP Instead of TCP
data.text: TCP is built into operating system kernels. Improving TCP requires updating every OS, which takes years. QUIC runs in user space, so protocol improvements can deploy to users much faster. QUIC adds its own reliability, congestion control, and encryption on top of UDP, so it is not less reliable than TCP.
Side-by-Side Comparison
Multiplexing Explained

Multiplexing is the feature that most directly improves real-world performance. In HTTP/1.1, a browser loading a page with 50 assets opens 6 to 8 parallel connections. In HTTP/2, all 50 requests travel over one connection. Fewer connections mean less CPU overhead, fewer packet retransmissions, and better use of available bandwidth.

data.caption: How multiplexing changes request delivery across HTTP versions
data.mermaid:
graph TD
    subgraph HTTP/1.1

        A2 -->|blocks| A3[Request 3]
        A3 -->|blocks| A4[Request 4]
    end
    subgraph HTTP/2

        B2 -->|interleaved| B3[Frame 3]
        B3 -->|interleaved| B4[Frame 4]
    end
    subgraph HTTP/3
        C1[Stream 1 lost] -.->|no impact| C2[Stream 2]
        C2 -.->|no impact| C3[Stream 3]
        C3 -.->|no impact| C4[Stream 4]
    end

data.text: TLS and Encryption Across Versions

Encryption is mandatory in HTTP/2 for all major browsers, meaning HTTP/2 effectively requires HTTPS. HTTP/3 goes further: TLS 1.3 is built into the protocol itself, and the handshake happens as part of the QUIC connection setup rather than as a separate layer.

This integration matters for performance. A full TLS 1.2 handshake over TCP requires two round trips before any application data can flow. QUIC with TLS 1.3 can complete the handshake in a single round trip, and on repeat connections, 0-RTT mode allows data to flow immediately.
When to Use Each Version

In practice, you rarely choose a single version. Modern servers and CDNs negotiate the best version each client supports. However, knowing the strengths and weaknesses of each version helps you configure servers and diagnose performance issues.

cards.title: HTTP/1.1
items: Legacy systems that cannot be upgraded
Debugging with raw tools like curl and telnet
Simple internal services with minimal asset loads
Always works, but expect lower throughput on complex pages

cards.title: HTTP/2
cards.description: The current production standard for most web traffic.
items: Standard web servers behind TLS-terminating proxies
APIs serving many small requests per connection
SSR and SSR frameworks where asset bundling still matters
Works on all modern browsers and requires HTTPS

cards.title: HTTP/3
cards.description: Best for lossy, mobile, and high-latency networks.
items: Mobile applications on unreliable cellular networks
Services where connection migration matters like VPNs
CDN edge nodes serving global traffic
Growing browser support; still not universal in enterprise environments

data.text: What HTTP/3 Means for Performance

The performance benefit of HTTP/3 is most visible on networks with packet loss. On a fast, reliable home connection, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 often feel identical. On a crowded cellular network where packets disappear regularly, QUIC's lack of transport-level head-of-line blocking can noticeably improve page load times and video streaming quality.

Connection migration is another underrated benefit. When you walk from your home Wi-Fi to a cellular network, your phone IP address changes. With TCP, all active connections break and must reconnect. With QUIC, the connection identifier stays the same, so ongoing downloads and API calls continue seamlessly.

data.title: Detecting HTTP Versions from the Command Line
data.code:
# Check the HTTP version of any endpoint
curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i "HTTP/"

# Output will show the negotiated version:
# HTTP/2 200
# or
# HTTP/3 200

# Force HTTP/1.1 to see the difference
curl --http1.1 -sI https://example.com | head -1

data.title: Server Push Is Not a Silver Bullet
data.text: HTTP/2 server push can improve performance when used carefully, but misconfigured push wastes bandwidth by sending resources the browser already cached. Modern practice favors resource hints like Link rel=preload over aggressive server push.
Common Misconceptions

items: HTTP/2 is not faster than HTTP/1.1 on every site. Asset bundling and caching matter more than protocol version for small sites.
QUIC over UDP is not less reliable than TCP. QUIC implements its own loss recovery and congestion control.
HTTP/3 does not eliminate all head-of-line blocking. Application-level head-of-line blocking, where a slow API call blocks a page, still exists.
Upgrading to HTTP/2 does not require code changes. Existing applications work transparently, though you may want to revisit asset bundling strategy.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections but still suffered from head-of-line blocking at the application layer.
HTTP/2 added multiplexing, binary framing, and HPACK header compression, requiring HTTPS in browsers.
HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC over UDP, eliminating transport-level head-of-line blocking and enabling faster connection migrations.
TLS 1.3 is built into HTTP/3, reducing handshake round trips and improving security by default.
Modern production should serve HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 through CDNs and reverse proxies; version negotiation happens automatically.
data.takeaway: Understanding the evolution from HTTP/1.1 through HTTP/3 gives you the vocabulary to explain performance regressions, choose optimal server configurations, and design APIs that work efficiently across all network conditions.

items.question: Do I need to rewrite my application to use HTTP/2?
items.answer: No. HTTP/2 is backward compatible at the application layer. Existing websites and APIs work without code changes. You may want to revisit asset bundling because multiplexing reduces the benefit of splitting files into many small chunks.

items.question: Why does HTTP/3 use UDP instead of TCP?
items.answer: TCP is implemented in operating system kernels, which makes protocol updates slow. QUIC runs in user space, so improvements deploy faster. QUIC adds its own reliability, congestion control, and encryption on top of UDP, making it comparable to TCP in reliability.

items.question: Is HTTP/3 faster than HTTP/2 in every scenario?
items.answer: No. On reliable, low-latency networks the difference is small. The biggest gains are on lossy mobile networks where TCP head-of-line blocking hurts most. On a fast home connection, you may not notice a difference.

items.question: Can I use HTTP/3 on my local development server?
items.answer: Yes, but it requires special configuration. Popular servers like nginx, Caddy, and cloud providers like Cloudflare and Vercel support HTTP/3. Local testing with curl or a browser that supports QUIC is possible but requires enabling the feature.

data.text: HTTP/3 is not about raw speed in ideal conditions. It is about keeping performance predictable when the network is imperfect.
